issues: Science: the book calls diseases spread by used syringes, blades or blood transfusion "non-communicable" and gives hepatitis A, B, C and AIDS as examples. In medicine these are infectious (communicable) diseases spread by blood or other routes; non-communicable diseases are ones such as diabetes, heart disease and cancer that do not pass from person to person at all. Hepatitis A also spreads mainly through contaminated food and water, not blood. Transcribed as printed.

decorative: Drawing of two patients in hospital beds, one with a drip stand, with charts hanging on the beds.
issues: Science: "drinking dirty water" is given as a way of catching a "non-communicable" disease; diseases spread by dirty water (such as hepatitis A and E, cholera and typhoid) are communicable. See the note on the previous page. Transcribed as printed. The book also mixes feminine and masculine verbs for "diseases" (لگتیں / لگ سکتے ہیں); kept as printed.

issues: Science: the book places the liver "in the upper part of the chest" (چھاتی کے بالائی حصے میں); it lies in the upper right abdomen, under the ribs. It also says the liver sends blood "back to the heart" after filtering, which is a simplification. The English and Pashto give the correct position (upper abdomen).

issues: Science: newborn jaundice is usually physiological (the baby's liver is still immature), not mainly "hereditary"; the book calls it a hereditary or internal cause. Transcribed as printed.

Health: medical guidance today advises against treating newborn jaundice by putting the baby in sunlight, and glucose drips or medicines are given only on a doctor's advice. A jaundiced newborn should be seen by a doctor. Transcribed as printed.

issues: Key points: AIDS is listed here as a "communicable disease" (متعدی مرض), although page 2 of the book gives AIDS as an example of a non-communicable disease. AIDS is in fact communicable (it spreads through blood and body fluids). The key point also says albumin "helps blood to clot"; page 4 lists albumin and the clotting proteins separately, which is correct (albumin itself does not clot blood). Transcribed as printed.

Exercise 1, MCQ 3: the expected answer follows the book's own (incorrect) classification of hepatitis as non-communicable; medically it is communicable. MCQ 4 prints "بیماریاں لگتی ہے" (plural noun, singular verb); kept as printed.

issues: Science: the involuntary (smooth) muscle examples include the heart, which has its own type (cardiac muscle, described next), and the "nervous system", which is not muscle; the lungs move by the breathing muscles rather than by muscle in the lungs themselves. Smooth muscle is found in the walls of the stomach, intestines, blood vessels, bladder and in the iris of the eye. Transcribed as printed.

issues: Cricket: for a right-handed batsman it is the other way round — an off-spinner's ball turns in (from off to leg), and a leg-spinner's ball turns away (from leg to off). Off spin is mostly bowled with the fingers and leg spin with the wrist. Transcribed as printed.

Key points: the no-ball definition here (whole foot over the crease, or a ball above the chest) differs slightly from the text on page 82; the Laws use "no part of the front foot behind the popping crease" and "above the waist on the full". Kept as printed.

issues: Measurements: some printed figures are rounded or slightly off — the penalty area is 18 × 44 yd (16.5 × 40.3 m), not "40 × 17 m"; the goal area is 6 × 20 yd (5.5 × 18.3 m); the corner arc has a radius of 1 yd, not a diameter; and posts are at most 5 in (12 cm) wide. The half-time break under the Laws of the Game is up to 15 minutes. Transcribed as printed.

It says penalties are for fouls "in the goal area"; under the Laws a penalty is given for a direct-free-kick foul by a defender inside their own penalty area. A squad size of "16 players" is the book's figure (squads vary by competition). Offside also requires the player to be in the opponents' half and involved in play. The tiny Urdu labels in the figure are rendered in English here. Transcribed as printed.
